Squat Guide

Learn how to squat with better form, track sets and volume, avoid common squat mistakes, and progress your lower-body training.

FORM GUIDE

How to do the Squat

  1. Set the bar securely on the upper back, brace your torso, and step out with a stable stance.
  2. Keep your feet rooted and let the knees track in the same direction as the toes.
  3. Sit down between your hips while keeping the chest tall and the midfoot balanced.
  4. Reach a depth you can control, then drive the floor away to stand up.
  5. Reset your breath and brace before each rep instead of rushing the set.
COMMON MISTAKES

Keep the lift honest

  • Letting the knees collapse inward as the load gets heavy.
  • Rising onto the toes and losing midfoot balance.
  • Relaxing the brace at the bottom of the rep.
  • Cutting depth shorter every week while counting it as progress.
HOW TO PROGRESS

Make progress measurable

  • Progress reps first, then load, while keeping depth consistent.
  • Use volume changes carefully because squat fatigue can affect the rest of the week.
  • Track RIR so a normal working set does not become an accidental max attempt.
  • If the lift stalls, adjust volume, pause work, or recovery before changing everything.

Use the workout volume calculator when sets, reps, or load change enough that recovery becomes harder to judge.

TRACKING TIPS

What to log in LogWise

  • Record stance notes, depth, belt use, and any form cues that changed the set.
  • Track total squat volume and compare it with leg press, lunges, and other leg work.
  • Review estimated 1RM over several weeks rather than reacting to one rough session.

If you want a paper structure first, the workout log template captures the same basics: sets, reps, weight, RIR, and notes.

LogWise cues

  • Knees should track over toes — don't let them cave inward.
  • Break parallel with the hips if your flexibility allows.
  • Inhale going down, exhale on the way up.
  • Keep heels on the ground throughout the entire movement.

Track the useful numbers

For this lift, the most useful history is simple: top set, back-off sets, total working volume, RIR, and short technique notes.
